sections.h2: Selling in a city of renters and owners
sections.html:
Garfield is a compact Bergen County city where renters outnumber owners, and its sale paperwork is priced by unit count. It has an estimated 33,353 residents in 2025 on 2.11 square miles of land, about 15,469 per square mile at the 2020 count.

Just 44.7% of households own their home (2020 to 2024). Median home value is $475,500 and median gross rent is $1,688. With that split, a seller tends to see two kinds of buyer: an occupant, and an investor who plans to rent the units out. Both face the same city paperwork before title passes, starting with the resale certificate.

Old neighborhood names such as Belmont, Bogart Heights, Dundee Dam and Plauderville still appear on deeds and listings. One piece of local history matters for due diligence: the EPA identified groundwater contamination from a 1983 chromic acid spill at a former electroplating company in Garfield and announced a $37 million cleanup in 2016. Buyers and lenders sometimes ask about nearby cleanup sites, so look up your street in the EPA's records early.

sections.h2: What Garfield requires before a resale
sections.html:
Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale plus a separate smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. Submit the request through the Building Department citizen portal or by email, then wait for the email that tells you when fees are due.

Processing takes 10 business days from the day the application is received, so do not schedule a closing until the certificate is in hand. Ignoring the ordinance can bring a fine of $2,000.

  • Send the property address and the full names, current home addresses, phone numbers and emails of buyer and seller. Do not list a business, attorney or real estate office address.
  • If an LLC or corporation is selling, give the contact person's details as well.
  • For an estate sale, attach the Surrogate letter to the application.
  • Pay the certificate fee to the City of Garfield and the smoke certification fee to the Bureau of Fire Prevention, each with its own check or money order.

Fees are charged by building type, and the city asks sellers to wait for its fee email before paying.

Garfield resale fees
Building typeCertificate of occupancySmoke and CO certification
One-family$50$50
Two-family$100$100
Three or more units$100 for the first two units, $25 per added unit$100 for the first two units, $25 per added unit

Each of these situations adds one step without blocking the sale. An as-is house can still receive its paperwork once the smoke and fire items pass.

The detector rules are specific. Ten-year sealed-battery smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms must sit within ten feet of every bedroom, and a common stairwell needs smoke alarms at the top and bottom. Inspectors also ask for access to the attic and basement.

  • A tenant-occupied house may also need a dwelling certificate. Ordinance 2213 requires one on any change of occupancy, with a $60 fee per unit that includes the smoke certification, unless an inspection happened within the previous eleven months.
  • A second visit costs another $60 per unit if the unit fails or the paperwork is not on site.
  • For a house with a deceased owner, the application asks for the Surrogate letter, so have it ready before you apply.

If repairs are the problem, fix the detector items first. They are the cheapest part of the checklist, and the state rule behind them is N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3.

sections.h2: State filings recorded with the deed
sections.html:
The Bergen County Clerk records a Garfield deed, and the state attaches two filings to it: the Realty Transfer Fee and a gross income tax residency form. The seller owes the fee, and it is computed from the consideration recited in the deed.

For prices of $350,000 or less, the schedule starts at $2.00 per $500 of the first $150,000 and tops out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A higher schedule applies above $350,000, opening at $2.90 per $500 and reaching $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000.

The state exempts deeds between husband and wife or parent and child, and an executor's deed distributing an estate to an heir. An arm's-length purchase fits none of these.

The residency paperwork is the GIT/REP. A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax, never less than 2% of the deed consideration, unless a listed assurance on the form applies. No deed gets recorded without a signed GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

sections.h2: Trains, roads and schools buyers ask about
sections.html:
Garfield sells on access: two NJ Transit rail stops and Route 46 both sit inside the city. The Garfield and Plauderville stations on the Bergen County Line run to Hoboken Terminal, with a transfer at Secaucus Junction for Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 160 and 161 run to the Port Authority terminal in Midtown Manhattan.

By road, U.S. Route 46 and County Route 507 pass through, and Midland Avenue, Outwater Lane, River Drive and Passaic Street are the other main streets. Mean commute time is 28.0 minutes. The public schools are Garfield Public Schools, a pre-K to grade 12 district. A buyer with children will ask, so have the district name ready.

sections.h2: Which sale route fits a Garfield owner?
sections.html:
Your deadline and the condition of the building decide it. Listing reaches the most buyers but puts showings and repair requests on you. A private sale or cash buyer trims the repair list, yet the city certificate and fire certification apply to all three.

  • List with an agent if the building is in good order and you can wait on a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Sell privately if a buyer is already lined up, such as a tenant, relative or neighbor.
  • Consider a cash offer for a building that needs work, carries tenants or belongs to an estate, and settle in the contract who orders the certificate and pays the $50 or $100 city fee.

Fix the closing date first, then count back 10 business days to learn the last day to file with the city.

faqs.q: Is an inspection mandatory when I sell in Garfield?
faqs.a: Yes. Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale and a smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. Processing takes 10 business days, so do not schedule a closing before the certificate is issued.

faqs.q: How much is the Garfield resale certificate?
faqs.a: One-family houses pay $50 and two-family houses pay $100. Bigger buildings pay $100 for two units plus $25 for each one after that. The Bureau of Fire Prevention charges its smoke and CO certification on the same scale.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in a Garfield sale?
faqs.a: The seller. The county recording officer collects the state fee at recording, and the amount scales with the price in the deed. Spouse-to-spouse and parent-to-child deeds carry an exemption.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Garfield house that I inherited and have not cleared up yet?
faqs.a: Yes, once you have the right papers. Garfield wants the Surrogate letter with the certificate application on an estate sale. Selling to an outside buyer is a taxable transfer, though an executor's deed to an heir is exempt.

faqs.q: Do I need a dwelling certificate if tenants live in the house?
faqs.a: Possibly. Ordinance 2213 calls for a dwelling certificate on a change of occupancy, at $60 per unit, unless the unit was inspected in the previous eleven months. Ask the Fire Prevention Bureau whether your tenant situation triggers it.
